intro: Welcome to C2! You already know every structure; now the goal is control. In this lesson you keep long lists and pairs balanced (to reduce, improve and train), write long noun phrases a reader can follow, and make sure every sentence has only one meaning, so nobody reads 'Walking into the office, the computer was already on' and pictures a walking computer.
teachingNotes: Chain recap in one line each, don't re-teach: c1-nominalisation (a noun phrase has one head noun; adjectives and noun modifiers go before it, in/of/on phrases and relative clauses after it; the verb agrees with the head) and c1-participle-advanced (the hidden subject of an opening participle clause must be the first noun after the comma: *Arriving late, the meeting had already started). At C2 there are no new forms: the point is control, precision and choice. Be honest that sentence length is partly style: a long sentence is fine if a reader can follow it the first time. Test only clear cases: a broken parallel form, a noun stack that hides its head, a sentence with two possible meanings.

Objective multi-clause-parallelism. Parallel structure = items joined by and/or/but, or by a pair (both … and, either … or, neither … nor, not only … but also), share the same grammatical form: to reduce costs, (to) improve quality and (to) train staff, or reducing, improving and training. Common error: *The project aims to reduce costs, improving quality and to train staff → The project aims to reduce costs, improve quality and train staff. Put 'to' once at the start or before every item; don't mix. Pairs: the same form after each half (both demanding and well paid, not *both demanding and pays well; either by transfer or in cash; She not only wrote the code but also tested it). Not only at the START of a sentence brings inversion (c1-inversion: Not only did she …); in mid-sentence there is none. Comparisons with than/as are parallel too (faster than driving, not *than to drive). In long sentences keep parallel clauses parallel (why …, what … and how …; who …, who … and who …) and repeat the linking word when items are long. Indonesian trap: mengurangi, meningkatkan, melatih keep one shape by themselves, so learners choose to/-ing/noun one verb at a time and mix them. Bridges: tidak hanya … tetapi juga = not only … but also; baik … maupun = both … and.

Objective clear-noun-phrases. Noun stacks (many nouns piled before the head) are hard to read: *the government new rural school teacher training funding policy → the government's new policy on funding teacher training in rural schools. Method: find the head (usually the last noun of the stack), put the owner ('s) and an adjective before it, move the details after it with a preposition (on, for, in, of, to) or ONE relative clause, and keep familiar two-word compounds together (teacher training, licence fee, school fees, online loan apps). Don't over-correct into of-chains (*the policy of the funding of the training of teachers). Indonesian trap: Indonesian puts the details after the head (kebijakan baru pemerintah tentang …), which causes two opposite mistakes: reversing everything into a noun stack, or translating every yang as 'which is' (*the app which is new which is from the startup which is in Bandung → the new app from a Bandung startup). Yang + adjective → adjective before the head; yang + place/owner → a short phrase after it. Grade rewrites on a clear head and correct prepositions, not on one wording.

Objective avoid-ambiguity: four kinds. (1) Dangling modifiers: the opening phrase's hidden subject must be the first noun after the comma, for -ing, V3, after/before + -ing and As + noun alike. Common error: *Walking into the office, the computer was already on → Walking into the office, I saw that the computer was already on (or When I walked into the office, the computer was already on). Also *As the team leader, the decision was mine → As the team leader, I made the decision. (2) Misplaced modifiers: only, almost, just, even, nearly limit the word right after them: We almost lost every client (lost none) vs We lost almost every client (lost most); Only Rina signed (nobody else) vs Rina signed only the contract (nothing else). Honest note: 'She only ate the cake' meaning 'only the cake' is completely normal in speech, where stress makes it clear; be strict in reports, contracts and instructions. (3) Unclear pronoun reference: When the manager met the consultant, she said … (who?) → repeat the noun or rebuild so only one person fits; for which/this pointing at a whole idea, use this + noun (This increase upset the client). Indonesian dia covers he and she, but he/she doesn't help when both people are women or both are men. (4) Attachment ambiguity: I saw the man with the binoculars (who had them?) → Using binoculars, I saw the man / I saw the man who had the binoculars.

Multi-clause control (objective multi-clause-parallelism): one sentence can combine a participle clause, a main clause, a relative clause and a subordinate clause (Having reviewed the figures, the board approved the budget, which had been cut by 10%, because sales had risen in every region). Habits: main subject and verb early and close together; each extra clause next to what it describes; long, new information at the end (end weight); parallel clauses for parallel ideas. Split into two sentences when there are two main messages, when the reader waits too long for the verb, or after about three clauses. Indonesian trap: formal Indonesian (laporan, surat dinas) chains yang … dan … sehingga … di mana …; di mana as an all-purpose link must not become 'where' (*The budget was cut, where the team had to … → so the team had to …). These are style guidelines: accept any clear, correct split or combination.

Limits and grading: no new grammar; every A0–C1 structure may appear. In typed answers accept any correct, clear alternative (checked the first chapter only = checked only the first chapter); commas, hyphens and capitals don't matter. All figures are practice figures. Contexts: ministries, universities (UGM, UI, ITB), NGOs, startups, offices in Jakarta, Bandung, Surabaya, Yogyakarta. British spelling (programme, licence, organised) with American programme/program, licence/license noted when relevant.

keyPoints.title: Parallel structure in lists, pairs and long sentences
keyPoints.explanation: Parallel structure means the items in a list or a pair have the same grammatical form: to reduce costs, improve quality and train staff (one to, three verbs), or reducing, improving and training. Put to once or before every item; don't mix. Pairs (both … and, either … or, neither … nor, not only … but also) need the same form after each half: both demanding and well paid. In long sentences, keep parallel clauses parallel: why it happened, what we learnt and how we will change.

examples.id: Proyek ini bertujuan mengurangi biaya, meningkatkan kualitas, dan melatih staf.

examples.id: Pekerjaan itu menuntut sekaligus bergaji bagus.

examples.id: Dia tidak hanya menulis kodenya, tetapi juga mengujinya.

id.title: Struktur paralel dalam daftar, pasangan dan kalimat panjang
id.explanation: Struktur paralel berarti semua bagian dalam daftar atau pasangan punya bentuk tata bahasa yang sama: to reduce costs, improve quality and train staff (satu to, tiga kata kerja), atau reducing, improving and training. Tulis to sekali di depan atau di depan setiap bagian; jangan dicampur. Pasangan (both … and, either … or, neither … nor, not only … but also) butuh bentuk yang sama setelah tiap bagian: both demanding and well paid. Di kalimat panjang, klausa yang sejajar juga harus sejajar bentuknya: why it happened, what we learnt and how we will change.

keyPoints.title: Long noun phrases that stay readable
keyPoints.explanation: Don't pile many nouns in front of the head noun (a noun stack): the government new rural school teacher training funding policy is hard to read. Find the head (usually the last noun: policy), put it early with the owner and an adjective before it, and move the details after it with a preposition or one relative clause: the government's new policy on funding teacher training in rural schools. One or two words before the head and one or two short phrases after it is plenty.

examples.en: the government's new policy on funding teacher training in rural schools
examples.id: kebijakan baru pemerintah tentang pendanaan pelatihan guru di sekolah-sekolah pedesaan

examples.en: the hospital's plan to recruit more night-shift nurses
examples.id: rencana rumah sakit untuk merekrut lebih banyak perawat shift malam

id.title: Noun phrase panjang yang tetap mudah dibaca
id.explanation: Jangan menumpuk banyak kata benda di depan kata inti (noun stack): the government new rural school teacher training funding policy sulit dibaca. Cari kata intinya (biasanya kata benda terakhir: policy), taruh di depan dengan pemilik dan kata sifat sebelumnya, lalu pindahkan detailnya ke belakang dengan kata depan (preposition) atau satu klausa relatif: the government's new policy on funding teacher training in rural schools. Satu atau dua kata sebelum kata inti dan satu atau dua frasa pendek sesudahnya sudah cukup.

keyPoints.title: Spotting and fixing ambiguity
keyPoints.explanation: A sentence is ambiguous when a reader can understand it in two ways. Four common causes: a dangling modifier (Walking into the office, the computer was already on), a misplaced only or almost (We almost lost every client is not We lost almost every client), an unclear pronoun (When the manager met the consultant, she said … who?) and an unclear attachment (I saw the man with the binoculars: whose binoculars?). Fix it by putting the doer after the comma, moving the small word next to what it limits, repeating the noun, or rewriting the phrase.

examples.en: Walking into the office, I saw that the computer was already on.
examples.id: Saat masuk ke kantor, saya melihat komputernya sudah menyala.

examples.en: When the manager met the consultant, the consultant said the budget was too small.
examples.id: Saat manajer bertemu konsultan, konsultan itulah yang bilang anggarannya terlalu kecil.

id.title: Menemukan dan memperbaiki ambiguitas
id.explanation: Kalimat ambigu kalau pembaca bisa memahaminya dengan dua cara. Empat penyebab umum: dangling modifier (Walking into the office, the computer was already on), only atau almost yang salah tempat (We almost lost every client tidak sama dengan We lost almost every client), kata ganti yang tidak jelas (When the manager met the consultant, she said … siapa?) dan frasa yang bisa menempel ke dua kata (I saw the man with the binoculars: teropong siapa?). Perbaiki dengan menaruh pelakunya tepat setelah koma, memindahkan kata kecil itu ke samping kata yang dibatasinya, mengulang kata bendanya, atau menulis ulang frasanya.

assessment.prompt:
One word breaks the parallel structure of this list. Write that word in the correct form:
The new manager wants to shorten meetings, simplify reports and improving communication between teams.

to improve

assessment.prompt:

assessment.prompt:

assessment.prompt:
Sari wrote this in a report about her first week at a new job. Fix the dangling modifier: write the two missing words (subject + verb).
Wrong: As a new employee, the rules were confusing.
Right: As a new employee, ___ ___ the rules confusing.
acceptableAnswers: i found
assessment.rubric: Correct: I found (Sari is the new employee, so I must come right after the comma; find + noun + adjective = think it is). 'I find' = 80 (correct structure, but the first week is past). 'I thought' or 'I considered' = 60 (the doer is fixed, but 'thought the rules confusing' sounds unnatural). 'the rules' / 'they were' = 0 (still dangling).

material.title: Parallel structure: the same form in lists and pairs

blocks.text:
**Parallel structure** means that the items in a list or a pair have the **same grammatical form**: all verbs, all -ing forms, all nouns, or all clauses. The reader sees the pattern at once and can follow even a long sentence.
- *The project aims **to reduce** costs, **improve** quality and **train** staff.* ✓ (one *to*, three verbs)
- *The project aims **to reduce** costs, **to improve** quality and **to train** staff.* ✓ (*to* before every item: a little more formal and emphatic)
- *The project aims to reduce costs, **improving** quality and **to train** staff.* ✗ (to + verb, -ing, to + verb: three different shapes)
**The rule for *to*:** write it once at the start, or before every item. Don't mix.
**Pairs** work the same way: *both … and*, *either … or*, *neither … nor*, *not only … but also*. What comes after the first word must match what comes after the second:
- *The job is **both demanding and well paid**.* ✓ (two adjectives), not *both demanding and pays well* ✗
- *You can pay **either by transfer or in cash**.* ✓ (two phrases with a preposition)
- *She **not only wrote** the code **but also tested** it.* ✓ (two verbs)
**Comparisons** with *than* and *as* follow it too: *Taking the train is faster than **driving*** (not *than to drive*).
**Why does 'Not only did she …' look different?** When *not only* **starts** the sentence, it brings inversion (you met it at C1: *Not only did she write the code, she also …*). In the middle of a sentence there is no inversion.
**Long sentences:** parallel clauses keep long items clear. Repeat the linking word when the items are long: *We need someone **who** is organised, **who** works well under pressure and **who** speaks Mandarin.*

id.text:
**Struktur paralel** berarti semua bagian dalam sebuah daftar atau pasangan punya **bentuk tata bahasa yang sama**: semuanya kata kerja, semuanya bentuk -ing, semuanya kata benda, atau semuanya klausa. Pembaca langsung melihat polanya, jadi kalimat panjang pun tetap mudah diikuti.
- *The project aims **to reduce** costs, **improve** quality and **train** staff.* ✓ (satu *to*, tiga kata kerja)
- *The project aims **to reduce** costs, **to improve** quality and **to train** staff.* ✓ (*to* di depan setiap bagian: sedikit lebih formal dan tegas)
- *The project aims to reduce costs, **improving** quality and **to train** staff.* ✗ (to + kata kerja, -ing, to + kata kerja: tiga bentuk berbeda)
**Aturan untuk *to*:** tulis sekali di awal, atau di depan setiap bagian. Jangan dicampur.
**Pasangan** juga begitu: *both … and*, *either … or*, *neither … nor*, *not only … but also*. Yang datang setelah kata pertama harus sama bentuknya dengan yang datang setelah kata kedua:
- *The job is **both demanding and well paid**.* ✓ (dua kata sifat), bukan *both demanding and pays well* ✗
- *You can pay **either by transfer or in cash**.* ✓ (dua frasa dengan kata depan)
- *She **not only wrote** the code **but also tested** it.* ✓ (dua kata kerja)
**Perbandingan** dengan *than* dan *as* juga mengikuti aturan ini: *Taking the train is faster than **driving*** (bukan *than to drive*).
**Kenapa 'Not only did she …' terlihat beda?** Kalau *not only* **membuka** kalimat, muncul inversi (sudah kamu pelajari di C1: *Not only did she write the code, she also …*). Di tengah kalimat tidak ada inversi.
**Kalimat panjang:** klausa yang paralel membuat bagian yang panjang tetap jelas. Ulangi kata penghubungnya kalau bagiannya panjang: *We need someone **who** is organised, **who** works well under pressure and **who** speaks Mandarin.*

blocks.text: **Indonesian trap:** in Indonesian, verbs in a list keep the same shape by themselves: *mengurangi biaya, meningkatkan kualitas, dan melatih staf*. English makes you choose a form (*to reduce*, *reducing*, *reduction*), and it's easy to choose again for each verb and end up mixing them. Choose the form **once**, for the first item, and copy it. Useful matches: *tidak hanya … tetapi juga* = **not only … but also**; *baik … maupun* = **both … and**; *atau … atau* = **either … or**.

id.text: **Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** dalam bahasa Indonesia, kata kerja dalam daftar otomatis punya bentuk yang sama: *mengurangi biaya, meningkatkan kualitas, dan melatih staf*. Bahasa Inggris memaksamu memilih bentuk (*to reduce*, *reducing*, *reduction*), dan gampang sekali memilih ulang untuk setiap kata kerja sehingga bentuknya tercampur. Pilih bentuknya **sekali saja**, untuk bagian pertama, lalu tiru. Padanan yang berguna: *tidak hanya … tetapi juga* = **not only … but also**; *baik … maupun* = **both … and**; *atau … atau* = **either … or**.

material.title: Long noun phrases that stay readable

blocks.text:
**Quick recap (C1):** a noun phrase is built around one main noun, the **head**, with words before it (*a significant*) and after it (*in online sales*). The verb agrees with the head.
**The C2 problem: noun stacks.** English *can* put nouns in front of nouns: *teacher training*, *school fees*, *a licence fee*. One or two is normal. Five or six in a row is a **noun stack**, and the reader has to get to the very end to find out what you're talking about:
- *the government new rural school teacher training funding policy* ✗
**How to unpack it:**
- **Step 1:** find the head. In a stack it's usually the **last noun**: *policy*.
- **Step 2:** put the owner and the adjective before it: *the government's new policy*.
- **Step 3:** move the rest **after** the head, with a preposition (*on, for, in, of, to*) or one relative clause: *on funding teacher training in rural schools*.
- **Step 4:** keep familiar pairs together (*teacher training* is fine).
Result: *the government's new policy on funding teacher training in rural schools* ✓
**Don't over-correct** into a chain of *of*: *the policy of the funding of the training of teachers* ✗ is just as hard to read. Aim for one or two words before the head and one or two short phrases after it.

id.text:
**Ulasan singkat (C1):** noun phrase dibangun di sekitar satu kata benda utama, **kata inti** (head), dengan kata-kata sebelumnya (*a significant*) dan sesudahnya (*in online sales*). Kata kerjanya mengikuti kata inti.
**Masalah di C2: tumpukan kata benda (noun stack).** Bahasa Inggris *boleh* menaruh kata benda di depan kata benda: *teacher training*, *school fees*, *a licence fee*. Satu atau dua itu biasa. Lima atau enam berturut-turut adalah **noun stack**, dan pembaca harus membaca sampai ujung dulu untuk tahu apa yang kamu bicarakan:
- *the government new rural school teacher training funding policy* ✗
**Cara mengurainya:**
- **Langkah 1:** cari kata intinya. Dalam tumpukan, biasanya **kata benda terakhir**: *policy*.
- **Langkah 2:** taruh pemilik dan kata sifat di depannya: *the government's new policy*.
- **Langkah 3:** pindahkan sisanya ke **belakang** kata inti, dengan kata depan (*on, for, in, of, to*) atau satu klausa relatif: *on funding teacher training in rural schools*.
- **Langkah 4:** pasangan yang sudah lazim biarkan tetap bersama (*teacher training* tidak apa-apa).
Hasilnya: *the government's new policy on funding teacher training in rural schools* ✓
**Jangan berlebihan** sampai jadi rantai *of*: *the policy of the funding of the training of teachers* ✗ sama sulitnya dibaca. Usahakan satu atau dua kata sebelum kata inti dan satu atau dua frasa pendek sesudahnya.

blocks.text:
**Indonesian trap:** Indonesian puts the details **after** the head: *kebijakan baru pemerintah tentang …*. That causes two opposite mistakes:
- reversing everything into English 'before the head' order, which builds a noun stack (*the government new … policy* ✗);
- translating every *yang* as *which is*: *the app which is new which is from the startup which is in Bandung* ✗ → *the new app from a Bandung startup* ✓.
The fix: *yang + adjective* → an adjective **before** the head (*yang baru* → *new*); *yang + place or owner* → a short phrase **after** the head (*yang ada di Bandung* → *in Bandung*); keep at most **one** real relative clause.

id.text:
**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** bahasa Indonesia menaruh detail **sesudah** kata inti: *kebijakan baru pemerintah tentang …*. Ini menyebabkan dua kesalahan yang berlawanan:
- membalik semuanya ke urutan 'sebelum kata inti' gaya Inggris, sehingga jadi noun stack (*the government new … policy* ✗);
- menerjemahkan setiap *yang* menjadi *which is*: *the app which is new which is from the startup which is in Bandung* ✗ → *the new app from a Bandung startup* ✓.
Cara memperbaikinya: *yang + kata sifat* → kata sifat **sebelum** kata inti (*yang baru* → *new*); *yang + tempat atau pemilik* → frasa pendek **sesudah** kata inti (*yang ada di Bandung* → *in Bandung*); pakai paling banyak **satu** klausa relatif yang sungguhan.

blocks.prompt: Which is the clearest English for 'program pelatihan bahasa Inggris baru perusahaan untuk staf penjualan'?
options: the company new sales staff English training programme
the company's new English training programme for sales staff
the programme which is new of training English of the company for the staff of sales
blocks.explain: Head = *programme*. The owner and the adjective go before it (*the company's new English training*), the people after it (*for sales staff*). The first option is a six-noun stack; the third follows the Indonesian order word by word. (programme = British, program = American.)

id.prompt: Mana bahasa Inggris yang paling jelas untuk 'program pelatihan bahasa Inggris baru perusahaan untuk staf penjualan'?
id.explain: Kata inti = *programme*. Pemilik dan kata sifat ada di depannya (*the company's new English training*), orangnya di belakang (*for sales staff*). Pilihan pertama adalah tumpukan enam kata benda; pilihan ketiga mengikuti urutan bahasa Indonesia kata per kata. (programme = Inggris/British, program = Amerika.)

id.title: Noun phrase panjang yang tetap mudah dibaca

material.title: Four kinds of ambiguity, and how to fix them

blocks.text:
A sentence is **ambiguous** when a reader can understand it in **two ways**. In conversation, the listener can ask what you mean. In a report or an email they can't, so check for these four:
**1. Dangling modifiers.** Recap (C1): the hidden subject of an opening phrase must be the first noun after the comma. That applies to every opening phrase, not only -ing ones: *Walking into the office, the computer was already on* ✗ (the computer walked in?) → *Walking into the office, **I** saw that the computer was already on* ✓. The same goes for *As the team leader, the decision was mine* ✗ → *As the team leader, **I** made the decision* ✓.
**2. Misplaced modifiers.** Small words like *only, almost, just, even, nearly* limit the word **right after** them:
- *We **almost lost** every client* = we didn't lose any (it nearly happened).
- *We lost **almost every** client* = we lost most of them.
- *Rina signed **only the contract*** = nothing else. ***Only Rina** signed the contract* = nobody else.
**3. Unclear pronouns.** *When the manager met the consultant, **she** said the budget was too small.* Who said it? Repeat the noun (*… **the consultant** said …*) or rebuild the sentence so only one person fits.
**4. Unclear attachment.** *I saw the man **with the binoculars**.* Did I use the binoculars, or did the man have them? Move or rewrite the phrase: ***Using binoculars**, I saw the man* / *I saw the man **who had** the binoculars*.

id.text:
Kalimat **ambigu** kalau pembaca bisa memahaminya dengan **dua cara**. Dalam percakapan, pendengar bisa bertanya maksudmu. Dalam laporan atau email tidak bisa, jadi periksa empat hal ini:
**1. Dangling modifier.** Ulasan (C1): subjek tersembunyi dari frasa pembuka harus menjadi kata benda pertama setelah koma. Ini berlaku untuk semua frasa pembuka, bukan hanya yang -ing: *Walking into the office, the computer was already on* ✗ (komputernya yang berjalan masuk?) → *Walking into the office, **I** saw that the computer was already on* ✓. Begitu juga *As the team leader, the decision was mine* ✗ → *As the team leader, **I** made the decision* ✓.
**2. Misplaced modifier (kata pembatas yang salah tempat).** Kata kecil seperti *only, almost, just, even, nearly* membatasi kata **tepat sesudahnya**:
- *We **almost lost** every client* = kami tidak kehilangan satu pun (hampir saja terjadi).
- *We lost **almost every** client* = kami kehilangan sebagian besar klien.
- *Rina signed **only the contract*** = tidak ada dokumen lain. ***Only Rina** signed the contract* = tidak ada orang lain.
**3. Kata ganti yang tidak jelas.** *When the manager met the consultant, **she** said the budget was too small.* Siapa yang bilang? Ulangi kata bendanya (*… **the consultant** said …*) atau susun ulang kalimatnya sehingga hanya satu orang yang cocok.
**4. Frasa yang bisa menempel ke dua kata.** *I saw the man **with the binoculars**.* Saya yang memakai teropong, atau pria itu yang membawa teropong? Pindahkan atau tulis ulang frasanya: ***Using binoculars**, I saw the man* / *I saw the man **who had** the binoculars*.

rows.en: Walking into the office, I saw that the computer was already on.
rows.id: Saat masuk ke kantor, saya melihat komputernya sudah menyala.

rows.id: Kami hampir kehilangan semua klien (tapi tidak jadi).

rows.id: Saat manajer bertemu konsultan, konsultan itulah yang bilang anggarannya terlalu kecil.

blocks.text:
**Indonesian trap:** *dia* means both *he* and *she*, so Indonesian writing often trusts the reader to guess who is meant. English *he/she* helps a little, but not when both people are women (*Bu Ani and Dr. Wulan*) or both are men. Also watch *which* or *this* after a long sentence: *The supplier delayed the delivery and raised its prices, which upset the client* (the delay, the prices, or both?). Name the idea with **this + noun**: *… and raised its prices. **This increase** upset the client.*
**Honest note:** *only* before the verb is completely normal in everyday speech (*I only had a coffee* = just a coffee), because your voice shows what you mean. Be strict about its position in reports, contracts and instructions.

id.text:
**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** *dia* berarti *he* sekaligus *she*, jadi tulisan berbahasa Indonesia sering membiarkan pembaca menebak siapa yang dimaksud. *He/she* dalam bahasa Inggris sedikit membantu, tapi tidak kalau kedua orangnya perempuan (*Bu Ani dan Dr. Wulan*) atau keduanya laki-laki. Hati-hati juga dengan *which* atau *this* setelah kalimat panjang: *The supplier delayed the delivery and raised its prices, which upset the client* (keterlambatannya, kenaikan harganya, atau keduanya?). Sebut idenya dengan **this + kata benda**: *… and raised its prices. **This increase** upset the client.*
**Catatan jujur:** *only* sebelum kata kerja sangat wajar dalam percakapan sehari-hari (*I only had a coffee* = cuma minum kopi), karena suaramu menunjukkan maksudnya. Tapi dalam laporan, kontrak dan instruksi, perhatikan posisinya dengan ketat.

blocks.prompt: Which sentence has only one possible meaning?
options: Pak Hasan discussed the problem with the new manager.
Pak Hasan and the new manager discussed the problem.
blocks.explain: In the first, *with the new manager* can attach to *discussed* (he talked to the manager) or to *the problem* (the problem is the manager!). Making the manager part of the subject leaves only one meaning.

id.prompt: Kalimat mana yang hanya punya satu arti?
id.explain: Pada kalimat pertama, *with the new manager* bisa menempel ke *discussed* (dia berdiskusi dengan manajer) atau ke *the problem* (masalahnya adalah si manajer!). Dengan menjadikan manajer bagian dari subjek, artinya tinggal satu.

id.title: Empat jenis ambiguitas dan cara memperbaikinya

material.title: Long sentences: build them well, or split them

blocks.text:
At C2 you can combine every kind of clause in one sentence:
*Having reviewed the figures, the board approved the budget, which had been cut by 10%, because sales had risen in every region.*
- *Having reviewed the figures* = participle clause (C1)
- *the board approved the budget* = **main clause**, the core: who did what
- *which had been cut by 10%* = relative clause, extra information about *the budget*
- *because sales had risen in every region* = subordinate clause, the reason
**Four habits keep a long sentence clear:**
- **Main subject and verb early and close together.** *The board, which met on Monday after a long delay caused by the elections in several provinces, approved …* makes the reader wait too long for the verb.
- **Each extra clause sits right next to what it describes** (*which* straight after *the budget*).
- **Long, new information goes at the end** ('end weight'): *The board is worried that the Surabaya branch has lost two managers in three months* reads better than *That the Surabaya branch has lost two managers in three months worries the board.*
- **Parallel ideas get parallel clauses:** *The report explains why …, what … and how …*
**When to split into two sentences:** when there are **two main messages**, when the reader has to hold the subject for too long, or when you need more than about three clauses. Splitting is a style choice, not a correction: if a reader can follow your sentence the first time, it can stay long.

id.text:
Di C2 kamu bisa menggabungkan semua jenis klausa dalam satu kalimat:
*Having reviewed the figures, the board approved the budget, which had been cut by 10%, because sales had risen in every region.*
- *Having reviewed the figures* = klausa partisip (C1)
- *the board approved the budget* = **klausa utama**, intinya: siapa melakukan apa
- *which had been cut by 10%* = klausa relatif, informasi tambahan tentang *the budget*
- *because sales had risen in every region* = klausa anak (subordinate clause), alasannya
**Empat kebiasaan agar kalimat panjang tetap jelas:**
- **Subjek utama dan kata kerjanya muncul awal dan berdekatan.** *The board, which met on Monday after a long delay caused by the elections in several provinces, approved …* membuat pembaca terlalu lama menunggu kata kerjanya.
- **Setiap klausa tambahan berada tepat di samping hal yang dijelaskannya** (*which* langsung setelah *the budget*).
- **Informasi yang panjang dan baru taruh di akhir** ('end weight'): *The board is worried that the Surabaya branch has lost two managers in three months* lebih enak dibaca daripada *That the Surabaya branch has lost two managers in three months worries the board.*
- **Ide yang sejajar pakai klausa yang sejajar:** *The report explains why …, what … and how …*
**Kapan memecah jadi dua kalimat:** kalau ada **dua pesan utama**, kalau pembaca harus mengingat subjeknya terlalu lama, atau kalau kamu butuh lebih dari sekitar tiga klausa. Memecah kalimat itu pilihan gaya, bukan koreksi: kalau pembaca bisa mengikuti kalimatmu pada bacaan pertama, kalimat itu boleh tetap panjang.

rows.en: Having reviewed the figures, the board approved the budget, which had been cut by 10%, because sales had risen in every region.
rows.id: Setelah meninjau angka-angkanya, dewan menyetujui anggaran, yang sudah dipotong 10%, karena penjualan naik di semua wilayah.
rows.note: participle + main + relative + reason: one clear core

id.note: partisip + utama + relatif + alasan: satu inti yang jelas

blocks.text: **Indonesian trap:** formal Indonesian (laporan, surat dinas) often links clause after clause with *yang, dan, sehingga, di mana*, and one sentence can run for five lines. Translated directly, it becomes an English sentence nobody can follow. Watch *di mana* in particular: as an all-purpose link it does **not** become *where*. *Where* is for places and situations (*the office where I work*, *a meeting where we agreed on the budget*), not for 'and so': *The budget was cut, **where** the team had to work faster* ✗ → *The budget was cut, **so** the team had to work faster* ✓.

id.text: **Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** bahasa Indonesia formal (laporan, surat dinas) sering menyambung klausa demi klausa dengan *yang, dan, sehingga, di mana*, sampai satu kalimat panjangnya lima baris. Kalau diterjemahkan langsung, jadilah kalimat bahasa Inggris yang tidak bisa diikuti siapa pun. Perhatikan terutama *di mana*: sebagai penghubung serba guna, *di mana* **tidak** menjadi *where*. *Where* untuk tempat dan situasi (*the office where I work*, *a meeting where we agreed on the budget*), bukan untuk 'sehingga': *The budget was cut, **where** the team had to work faster* ✗ → *The budget was cut, **so** the team had to work faster* ✓.

blocks.prompt: Which version is easier to follow?
options: The new clinic, which a foundation whose director, Dr. Wulan, has worked in Papua for ten years funded, opened in Jayapura last month.
The new clinic opened in Jayapura last month. It was funded by a foundation whose director, Dr. Wulan, has worked in Papua for ten years.
blocks.explain: The first puts a clause inside a clause between *the clinic* and *opened*, so the reader waits too long for the main verb. The second gives the main news first and moves the background into a second sentence.

id.prompt: Versi mana yang lebih mudah diikuti?
id.explain: Versi pertama menaruh klausa di dalam klausa di antara *the clinic* dan *opened*, jadi pembaca terlalu lama menunggu kata kerja utamanya. Versi kedua memberi berita utamanya dulu dan memindahkan latar belakangnya ke kalimat kedua.

assessment.ccs-1:
Ada satu kata yang merusak struktur paralel dalam daftar ini. Tulis kata itu dalam bentuk yang benar:
The new manager wants to shorten meetings, simplify reports and improving communication between teams.
assessment.ccs-2:
Tulis bentuk yang benar dari kata kerja dalam kurung supaya kedua bagiannya sejajar:
Dr. Wulan not only teaches at UGM but also ___ (run) a small NGO in Yogyakarta.
assessment.ccs-3:
Tumpukan kata benda ini sulit dibaca. Uraikan: lengkapi bagian kosong dengan tiga kata bahasa Inggris (kata kerja + dua kata benda).
the Surabaya port container capacity expansion plan
→ the plan to ___ at Surabaya port
assessment.ccs-4:
Tulis ini dalam bahasa Inggris yang wajar sebagai SATU noun phrase yang jelas. Mulai dengan 'the new report' dan jangan pakai 'which is':
laporan baru yang ditulis oleh tim yang ada di Surabaya
assessment.ccs-5:
Kalimat ini tidak jelas: siapa yang bilang? Yang bilang adalah Dr. Wulan. Tulis dua kata yang seharusnya menggantikan 'she':
When Bu Ani met Dr. Wulan at the ministry, she said the grant had been approved.
assessment.ccs-6:
Kalimat ini masuk ke laporan audit resmi, dan artinya harus: Budi memeriksa bab pertama saja, tidak ada yang lain. Tambahkan 'only' di tempat yang paling jelas dan tulis kalimat lengkapnya dalam bahasa Inggris:
Budi checked the first chapter.
assessment.ccs-7:
Sari menulis ini dalam laporan tentang minggu pertamanya di pekerjaan baru. Perbaiki dangling modifier-nya: tulis dua kata yang hilang dalam bahasa Inggris (subjek + kata kerja).
